Content:
Sometimes, we need to combine multiple rules of differentiation to differentiate a given function. As a reminder, the product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule are stated below.

Content:
- Product rule: [MATH: \hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(x) \cdot v(x) \right] = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)]
- Quotient rule: [MATH: \hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} \right] = \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}]
- Chain rule: [MATH: \hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(v(x)) \right] = u'(v(x))\cdot v'(x)]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we express [MATH: y] as a composite function

[MATH: y = u^4, \qquad u = \cos{v}, \qquad v = 2x.]

Differentiating gives

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 4u^3,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d v} = -\sin{v},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm d x} = 2.]

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (dy)/(du) ⋅ (du)/(dx); = (dy)/(du) ⋅ (du)/(dv) ⋅ (dv)/(dx); = 4u^{3} ⋅ (− \sin v) ⋅ (2); = 4(\cos 2x)^{3} ⋅ (− \sin 2x) ⋅ (2); = − 8\cos^{3} 2x\sin 2x.]

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: f(x) = e^{-2x}\tan({x^2})], then what is [MATH: f'(x)?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: f(x) = e^{-2x}\tan({x^2})], then what is [MATH: f'(x)?]

sections.normalized_html:
This question requires the product rule. Let [MATH: u(x) = e^{-2x}] and [MATH: v(x)=\tan{(x^2)}.] Then

[MATH: u'(x) = -2e^{-2x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2x\sec^2(x^2).]

Note that we used the chain rule to calculate both [MATH: u'(x)] and [MATH: v'(x).]

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

[MATH: f^{′}(x)|= u^{′}(x) ⋅ v(x) + u(x) ⋅ v^{′}(x); = (− 2e^{− 2x}) ⋅ \tan (x^{2}) + e^{− 2x} ⋅ 2x\sec^{2} (x^{2}); = 2e^{− 2x}(− \tan (x^{2}) + x\sec^{2} (x^{2})); = 2e^{− 2x}(x\sec^{2} (x^{2}) − \tan (x^{2})).]

items.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

sections.normalized_html:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator [MATH: u(x)=e^{3x}] and the denominator [MATH: v(x)=2^x +1.]

Differentiating [MATH: u(x)] and [MATH: v(x),] we have

[MATH: u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2^x \ln 2.]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate [MATH: u.]

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

[MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \ &=\dfrac{3e^{3x} \cdot \left( 2^{x}+1\right) - e^{3x} \cdot \left(2^x \cdot \ln2\right)}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\ &=\dfrac{3e^{3x}2^{x} + 3e^{3x} - e^{3x}2^{x}\ln 2}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\ &=\dfrac{e^{3x} \left( 3(2^{x}) - 2^{x} \ln 2 +3\right)}{\left(2^{x}+1 \right)^2} }]
sections.readable_text:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator [MATH: u(x)=e^{3x}] and the denominator [MATH: v(x)=2^x +1.]

Differentiating [MATH: u(x)] and [MATH: v(x),] we have

[MATH: u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2^x \ln 2.]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate [MATH: u.]

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	&= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \
&=\dfrac{3e^{3x} \cdot \left( 2^{x}+1\right) - e^{3x} \cdot \left(2^x \cdot \ln2\right)}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\
&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}2^{x} + 3e^{3x} - e^{3x}2^{x}\ln 2}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\
&=\dfrac{e^{3x} \left( 3(2^{x}) - 2^{x} \ln 2 +3\right)}{\left(2^{x}+1 \right)^2}
}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Sometimes, we need to combine multiple rules of differentiation to differentiate a given function. As a reminder, the product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule are stated below.

Content:
- Product rule: [MATH: \hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(x) \cdot v(x) \right] = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)]
- Quotient rule: [MATH: \hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} \right] = \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}]
- Chain rule: [MATH: \hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(v(x)) \right] = u'(v(x))\cdot v'(x)]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule

Example Prompt:
Differentiate [MATH: y = \cos^4{2x}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we express [MATH: y] as a composite function

[MATH: y = u^4, \qquad u = \cos{v}, \qquad v = 2x.]

Differentiating gives

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 4u^3,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d v} = -\sin{v},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm d x} = 2.]

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (dy)/(du) ⋅ (du)/(dx); = (dy)/(du) ⋅ (du)/(dv) ⋅ (dv)/(dx); = 4u^{3} ⋅ (− \sin v) ⋅ (2); = 4(\cos 2x)^{3} ⋅ (− \sin 2x) ⋅ (2); = − 8\cos^{3} 2x\sin 2x.]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: f(x) = e^{-2x}\tan({x^2})], then what is [MATH: f'(x)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
This question requires the product rule. Let [MATH: u(x) = e^{-2x}] and [MATH: v(x)=\tan{(x^2)}.] Then

[MATH: u'(x) = -2e^{-2x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2x\sec^2(x^2).]

Note that we used the chain rule to calculate both [MATH: u'(x)] and [MATH: v'(x).]

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

[MATH: f^{′}(x)|= u^{′}(x) ⋅ v(x) + u(x) ⋅ v^{′}(x); = (− 2e^{− 2x}) ⋅ \tan (x^{2}) + e^{− 2x} ⋅ 2x\sec^{2} (x^{2}); = 2e^{− 2x}(− \tan (x^{2}) + x\sec^{2} (x^{2})); = 2e^{− 2x}(x\sec^{2} (x^{2}) − \tan (x^{2})).]

Item 8 — Example: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: y =\dfrac{e^{3x}}{2^{x}+1},] find [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator [MATH: u(x)=e^{3x}] and the denominator [MATH: v(x)=2^x +1.]

Differentiating [MATH: u(x)] and [MATH: v(x),] we have

[MATH: u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2^x \ln 2.]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate [MATH: u.]

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	&= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \
&=\dfrac{3e^{3x} \cdot \left( 2^{x}+1\right) - e^{3x} \cdot \left(2^x \cdot \ln2\right)}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\
&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}2^{x} + 3e^{3x} - e^{3x}2^{x}\ln 2}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\
&=\dfrac{e^{3x} \left( 3(2^{x}) - 2^{x} \ln 2 +3\right)}{\left(2^{x}+1 \right)^2}
}]
